newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's new parliament gets down to work.
newsitem.headline: Albania's new parliament gets down to work.

text.p: Albania's newly-elected parliament starts work on Thursday on selecting a president and government to try to restore normality to the Balkan country after months of chaos early this year.

Albanians fired looted Kalashnikovs into the air to celebrate the resignation of Sali Berisha, president since 1992 but increasingly discredited since disputed elections last year and the collapse of get-rich-quick investment schemes.

"Even my wife who has heart trouble was cured today," said independent deputy Vladimir Fejzo, from the southern port of Vlore, flashpoint of February riots following the collapse of the pyramid schemes which Berisha admitted doing too little to control.

Wednesday's opening session of parliament observed a minute's silence for more than 1,500 people killed in the violence. Western diplomats including the U.S. ambassador were present, though they had stayed away from the opening of the previous parliament.

A million weapons were looted from armouries at the start of the rebellion and security at parliament was tight, with armed and plain clothes police surrounding the building and an armoured personnel carrier parked nearby.

Deputies from Berisha's Democratic Party, apart from secretary-general Genc Pollo, boycotted the session to protest at the conduct of the latest elections, described by international monitors as acceptable, if far from perfect.

Dritero Agolli, who opened the session as the oldest MP, refused Pollo permission to speak, saying the institutions of the parliament were still not elected. A commission must verify the mandate of each deputy.

Following constitutional court rulings on disputes and some changing of alliances, the Socialists and their coalition allies will have 118 seats in the 155-seat parliament, while the Democrats have 24. Seven deputies are women.
Parliament wass expected to elect Socialist Party secretary general Rexhep Mejdani to replace Berisha. He said he welcomed Berisha's resignation, though he regretted it had not come sooner.
"There was no other way out (for Berisha) because otherwise he could have lost his deputy's mandate as well," Mejdani said.

Berisha, a former communist heart surgeon, was initially praised in the West for quickly introducing market reforms. Enthusiasm faded as he resorted to increasingly authoritarian methods and failed to check the spread of the pyramid schemes.

His government resigned in March and was replaced by a Socialist-led national unity administration. The new assembly inherits the task of restoring law and order and resolving the economic chaos left by the collapse of the pyramid schemes.

"I will do the utmost for Vlore, every action should start from there. The essence of my duty to my voters in this parliament is to demand the maximum compensation for losses in pyramid schemes," Fejzo said.
Berisha's defiant resignation letter contended that the new parliament marked "the return to power of the last communist nomenklatura."
"The hours to come will give the possibility to all Albanians coldbloodedly to consider once again the five years of democracy and the five months of rebellion," he said.

Democracy has shaky foundations in Albania, where Stalinist leader Enver Hoxha ruled with an iron fist for 40 years until his death in April 1985, crushing opposition and isolating his state under a policy of self-reliance.
His successor, communist president Ramiz Alia, ruled out change but anti-government demonstrations from July 1990 led to reforms, culminating in multi-party elections in March 1991.
